We can determine the rough distribution and location of dark matter. It's not just random matter that's added to the universe somewhere, somehow. Its effects are directly visible which is how it was first detected, it's just it itself that we have trouble 'seeing' - though there are some pending studies to verify a supposed direct detection of it.

If it were baryonic matter, we'd be able to detect it. A big thing about dark matter is that it only interacts with things gravitationally. Anything that interacts in other ways has a far greater influence on light/radiation which tends to give itself away pretty easily. It's not just a few rocks here and there that we're looking for - the ratio of dark to baryonic matter in our Milky Way alone is around 10:1.

I was just thinking that, for the same amount of matter occupying the same total volume, clumping it up into rock balls rather than having it spread out evenly would reduce its "optical density" without changing the gravitational density.

No idea what the distribution is, though, so maybe it's impossible. I just like the mental picture of empty space being packed with tiny worldlets scooting around on different trajectories instead of being boring ol' diffuse gas.

It seems to me that both would have a detectable impact on visibility. Light that would go through field after field of these things, be they balls or gases, would dim. And the dimming would be dependent, but predictable, based upon the length and approximate density of dark matter regions it passes through. But this is not the case.

I wouldn't think of dark matter as diffuse gas for the same reason. Gas can be detected. The current top theory for dark matter is WIMPs or weakly interacting massive particles. They're big boys, by particle standards, that only meaningfully interact through gravity. Even if somehow you pile billions of particles in the dark matter into a single little compressed area, the only detection possible would be gravitational. Aside from the gravitational impact, light and anything else would pass right through them.
How do you know the light would dim and not instead be excited and amplified?

The most straight forward way to think of light is as a quantity of energy. The apparent brightness of something is going to vary based primarily on how much of that energy gets to you. When it hits things, some of that energy is going to get absorbed and some of its going to get reflected. The net effect is a decrease. For instance this is how we've been detecting exoplanets. We look at the apparent brightness of a star over a period of time. If there's a planet orbiting the star, we can detect a repeating or periodic tiny dip in apparent brightness each time the planet transits in front of the star relative to our view of it.
